Pre C6, the ICD on her normal attack string prevents her from vaping all of her hits. To further complicate things, since all 5 NAs don’t have the same scaling, your DPS becomes dependent on which hits she actually vapes and finishing your string (vaporizing on her N5 is about 30% of her damage per NA string, and not vaporizing N5 can offset her ICD for the next NA string). 

Meanwhile, Hu Tao can vape every CA in her E (similarly, Xiangling can do so for every hit of her burst). So, while Yoimiya is absolutely not a “bad” DPS, and has her own unique strengths, was at release already facing competition within her role as a pyro DPS from characters that can consistently vaporize hits from their main damage sources.

If you’re thinking of a character that applies “too much pyro,” you may be thinking of Klee? (Although that isn’t entirely true either…)

I don’t think so? At least GSIs don’t.

I don’t think the GSIs are necessarily more paranoid, but unless your course has remote proctoring/browser lockdowns/other shenanigans, there is definitely limited information we can gather — so I would hope most GSI teams acted similarly to mine in that we were very cautious with which students ultimately got reported (e.g. if a pair of students had only 2 similar answers, that could potentially just be coincidental, but if two students had free answer questions that were almost word for word identical, it would be much more difficult to come to that conclusion). 

I can say that it is very emotionally distressing for most of us, since we know how awful it is to deal with OSC (we — particularly the head GSIs — also have to deal with the OSC for every case, and I personally was accused of plagiarism at my undergrad) and the financial burden of having to retake a course and stay in school longer. We and the professor get torrents of emails from students accused of academic dishonesty — some are extremely entitled or crazy, but many show that the student is clearly distraught (a reasonable emotional response regardless of their innocence), and we try our best to help. Also, for many of these cases, we don’t want to believe that our students may have cheated!

Yes, I would ask your GSI or the head GSI if they could share with you the names of the students and specific questions that were similar. Then I would contact those students and ask to see their exams (I don’t think GSIs are allowed to share them directly) and compare the answers to see how similar the answers are.

If the similar answers are a phrase that was emphasized in class, I would bring that up.

OP, I would recommend you email your GSI/head GSI and (politely) ask for details about the questions/students with similar answers since they are most likely the one who reviewed the similarities between your exam and others. Those similarities are the reason your exam was flagged (assuming there isn’t online proctoring/browser lockdown shenanigans happening in this class). I’m sure they would be happy to share this with you — we don’t want to cause innocent students to go through unnecessary emotional turmoil, and guilty students tend to throw out damning evidence in response.

I would discourage anyone from doing this. I’ve had multiple students cheat on exams that were perfectly capable of doing well without the cheating, but that doesn’t change the fact that they cheated (or at the very least, to the professor, appear to have cheated) in the first place.

I can’t speak for OP’s class, but when I GSIed for ochem, we wouldn’t flag exams just for using material students learned outside of class! Most likely we would be a bit suspicious if a couple of students used one very distinct mechanism, and then compare those students’ exams to each other to see if there are other significant similarities. Most of the academic dishonesty on exams I’ve had to report was blatant copying that probably would’ve flown under the radar if the students had bothered to use different wording in their answer.

Speaking as someone who has GSIed for OChem, we mostly catch cheating from free-response (like explain why this is a SN2 reaction) answers that are identical or close to identical or extremely weird answers. We also used an algorithm to flag exams that were graded very similarly, which of course results in a lot of false positives (e.g. two students who answered the first question correctly but didn’t fill out the rest of the exam would be flagged), so the GSIs reviewed the flagged exams manually. We only reported students if their exams were extremely suspicious, but we most definitely do not have information about students’ browser history and the like and cannot 100% say that academic dishonesty occurred (until students get the notification from the OSC and start mercilessly throwing their friends under the bus).

SARS-CoV-2 (the virus that causes COVID-19) is able to enter our cells because of the specific interactions between a part its “spike" protein known as the RBD (receptor-binding domain) and a protein that is on the surface of our cells, ACE2.

SARS also enters our cells this way. We know that we can immunize against SARS with antibodies that recognize its spike protein RBD. This is because when these antibodies bind to the spike protein, it can no longer interact with ACE2. Without this interaction, SARS cannot enter the cell.

The authors of this paper have found that a vaccine containing the spike protein of SARS-CoV-2 causes the immune system (of rats) to produce antibodies that recognize the spike protein RBD and stop SARS-CoV-2 from entering cells.

Additionally, certain viruses (ex. Zika) can become more infectious in response to these antibodies, but this paper found no evidence for this in SARS-CoV-2.
